title: India was the first to land near the Moon's south pole
body: On 23 August 2023 the Chandrayaan-3 lander touched down at about 69 degrees south, closer to the lunar south pole than any craft before it. India became the fourth country to make a soft landing on the Moon. The mission cost roughly 75 million dollars.
takeaway: The polar region matters because its permanently shadowed craters hold water ice, a resource for future bases.
visual: a gold-foiled lunar lander with a small six-wheeled rover rolling down its ramp onto grey cratered ground, long shadows

title: India reached Mars on its first try, for less than a film budget
body: The Mars Orbiter Mission, Mangalyaan, entered orbit around Mars on 24 September 2014. India was the first Asian country to get there and the first country to succeed at its first attempt. The mission cost about 74 million dollars. The space film Gravity cost about 100 million.
takeaway: Built to last six months, the orbiter kept working for eight years.
visual: a small boxy spacecraft with a single solar panel approaching a rust-red planet against the stars

title: Saturn's rings are wider than Jupiter and thinner than a house is tall
body: The main rings stretch about 280,000 km from edge to edge, yet in most places they are only around 10 metres thick. They are made of countless lumps of water ice, from dust grains to boulders, each in its own orbit.
takeaway: Data from the Cassini probe suggest the rings may be only a few hundred million years old, though some scientists dispute that.
visual: a razor-thin band of icy rings seen edge-on beside a huge pale gold planet, tiny ice boulders glinting in the foreground

title: The Sun turns four million tonnes of itself into energy every second
body: In the Sun's core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium, and a little mass becomes energy. That adds up to roughly 4 million tonnes a second. The Sun is so large, holding 99.86% of the solar system's mass, that it has enough fuel for about 5 billion more years.
takeaway: All the sunlight Earth receives is a tiny sliver of that output, less than one part in two billion.
visual: the blazing surface of the Sun with arcs of plasma leaping from it, a tiny dot of a planet far to one side

title: Pluto has not completed one orbit since it was discovered
body: Clyde Tombaugh found Pluto in February 1930. It takes 248 Earth years to circle the Sun, so its first full lap since discovery will end in 2178. At 2,377 km across it is smaller than our Moon.
takeaway: In 2006 it was reclassified as a dwarf planet, because it shares its region of space with many similar icy bodies.
source: NASA New Horizons mission; International Astronomical Union
visual: a small pale world with a heart-shaped plain of ice on its surface, the distant Sun no more than a bright star

title: The Webb telescope hides behind a sunshade the size of a tennis court
body: The James Webb Space Telescope orbits 1.5 million km from Earth. Its 6.5-metre mirror is made of 18 beryllium segments coated in a film of gold weighing about 48 grams in all. A five-layer shield keeps the instruments colder than minus 220 degrees Celsius.
takeaway: It sees infrared light, so it must be very cold: a warm telescope would be blinded by its own glow.
visual: a space telescope with a honeycomb of golden hexagonal mirrors above a wide silver kite-shaped sunshield in deep space

title: The Moon has a far side, but not a dark side
body: The Moon turns once for every orbit of Earth, so we always see the same face. The far side gets just as much sunlight as the near side. Nobody had seen it until a Soviet probe photographed it in 1959. China made the first landing there in 2019.
takeaway: Earth's gravity slowed the Moon's spin until one face locked towards us. Most large moons are locked the same way.
visual: the heavily cratered far side of the Moon in full sunlight with the small blue Earth just rising beyond its edge

title: About 40,000 pieces of tracked junk are circling Earth
body: Space agencies track roughly 40,000 objects in orbit, of which only about 11,000 are working satellites. Over a million fragments larger than 1 cm are too small to follow. In low orbit they travel at around 28,000 km/h, so even a fleck of paint can chip a window.
takeaway: The Space Station regularly fires its engines to dodge debris. A serious collision could create thousands more pieces.
source: European Space Agency, Space Environment Report (2025)
visual: the curve of the Earth surrounded by a faint swarm of glinting fragments and dead satellites

title: Saturn's moon Titan has rain, rivers and seas, but not of water
body: Titan is the only moon with a thick atmosphere, and its surface is about minus 180 degrees Celsius. There, methane and ethane are liquid. They fall as rain and fill lakes and seas. The Huygens probe landed there in 2005, the most distant landing ever made.
takeaway: Titan is the only other world known to have liquid on its surface. NASA plans to send a drone, Dragonfly, to fly there.
visual: an orange hazy landscape with a dark still lake and rounded pebbles on the shore, a ringed planet dim in the sky

title: The echo of the Big Bang was first mistaken for pigeon droppings
body: In 1964 Arno Penzias and Robert Wilson could not get rid of a faint hiss in their radio antenna. They even scrubbed out the pigeon nests inside it. The hiss was the cosmic microwave background, light released about 380,000 years after the universe began.
takeaway: It won them the 1978 Nobel Prize and remains the strongest evidence that the universe had a hot, dense beginning.
visual: two engineers beside a huge horn-shaped radio antenna on a hillside, a pair of pigeons perched on its rim
